finding: The release's central safety argument is factually false about the code, and this repository's own corpus refutes it. §2 says 'Audit rows carry severity from the same error|warning|info vocabulary the schema requires, and audit_schema.go rejects a row that omits it. Nothing new is asserted by the agent being measured.' Measured: internal/cli/audit_schema.go only WRITES the sentence '- severity: field MUST exist; null for PASS, one of error|warning|info' into the prompt (line 24); no code path validates it. countAuditFindings (internal/cli/audit_record.go:228-257) validates category via invalidCategoryRows and never looks at severity. Across all 10,435 recorded audit rows in spec/.tp-review/, 67 non-PASS rows carry a severity OUTSIDE the claimed enum: high 16, medium 15, low 36, in cycles 0.29.0, 0.30.0, 0.31.0, 0.31.2 and 0.32.0 (0.32.0 alone has 24 low, 6 medium, 4 high). So the field the whole release gates on is unvalidated, and the corpus already contains values `blocking` has no rule for. The irony is recorded in the code: audit_record.go:259-270 explains that invalidCategoryRows exists precisely because 'tp renders the enum into every auditor prompt ... in words that promise unknown values are rejected -- and then never looked at what came back'. §2 makes that same mistake about the neighbouring field.
suggestion: Delete the false clause. Then either (a) make it true in this release -- add a record-time severity validator mirroring invalidCategoryRows, rejecting an absent severity, a non-PASS row with null severity, and any value outside error|warning|info, with a §7 test that a bad row is refused; or (b) state explicitly how `blocking` classifies an absent, null or out-of-enum severity on a non-PASS row, and add a §7 test pinning that. Without one of the two, `audit_converge_on=blocking` has an undefined case that 67 recorded rows already occupy.

finding: 'blocking' is never defined for audit severities, so tests 2 and 3 cannot be written from §2 alone. §2 says blocking 'counts a round clean when no surviving non-PASS row carries a blocking severity' without ever saying which of error|warning|info is blocking. The only clue is a parenthetical in §2.1's table ('r2, r3 carry zero error') and the wording of §7 tests 2-3 -- i.e. the tests define the term the spec was supposed to define. §2 also claims audit_converge_on 'takes the same two values on the same terms' as review_converge_on; that is false at the level that matters. Review grades a 4-value scale and blocks on critical|high (internal/cli/review.go:1973: 'critical or high severity under review_converge_on=blocking'); audit grades a 3-value enum. 'The same terms' cannot hold across two different partitions of two different vocabularies.
suggestion: State the audit blocking set as a literal in §2 -- e.g. 'blocking = {error}; warning and info are advisory' -- and replace 'the same two values on the same terms' with the explicit mapping, naming that the two phases use different severity vocabularies and therefore different blocking sets. A named constant pair (AuditConvergeOnBlocking/All plus an AuditSeverityBlocking predicate) is the twin of engine/reviewconvergeon.go the section claims to be.

finding: §4 and §7 test 4 give different answers on this repository's own recorded data, so one of them must fail. §4 requires that a spec_hash differing from the previous round's resets the streak. Measured in spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json: audit round 8 carries spec_hash sha256:1259a4af... and round 9 carries sha256:54e031e6... -- the spec moved between the only two clean rounds of that cycle. So under §4 the streak is reset at round 9 and `all` converges at round 10, not round 9. Test 4 asserts `all` converges 'at round 9, reproducing the recorded history exactly', and §2.1 rests its opt-in argument on that same 'exactly'. With §4 active the recorded history is NOT reproduced. (v0.36.0 has the same hazard: 8 distinct spec hashes across its 13 recorded audit rounds.)
suggestion: Decide and say which rule the replay runs under. Either state that test 4's replay evaluates the severity predicate ONLY, with §4's reset explicitly out of scope for that test, and re-word §2.1's 'reproduces the recorded history exactly' to 'reproduces the recorded finding counts exactly, ignoring the §4 reset'; or keep them composed and correct the expected values to blocking=round 3 / all=round 10, adding a third test that the v0.35.0 r8-to-r9 hash change is what moves the number. Either way §4 should carry the observation that tp's own converging cycle changed its spec between its two clean rounds -- that is the release's motivating defect occurring in its own evidence.

finding: Rule (2) of §5a -- 'A PASS carrying such a statement is an unresolved item for convergence, not a clean one' -- has no detectable subject, and under the only field that exists today no fixture in this repository can ever produce a clean round. §5a says the two changes touch nothing on the checklist and names no field, no marker and no detection rule for 'my prose knows something my verdict cannot carry'. The only free-text field on an audit row is `notes` (audit_schema.go:25, max 500 chars, 'always'). Measured on the four rounds §5a itself cites (spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/audit-round-10..13.ndjson): 100% of PASS rows carry a non-empty note -- 82/82, 83/83, 82/82, 81/81 -- and 74/74 spec-coverage PASS rows in every one of the four. So the mechanizable reading of rule (2) makes every round unclean forever and pins spec_coverage_clean_rounds at 0 permanently. §5a's own claim 'On the second rule none of the four rounds named above was clean' is therefore true by construction and cannot fail -- it is a restatement, not evidence.
suggestion: Name the carrier and the predicate, or move rule (2) to §6. The cheap shape: a new optional row key (e.g. `unrecorded_observation`: string|null, with the recommendation required when non-null, since §5a's own fifth case shows a bare note sits unactioned) and a stated convergence rule 'a PASS row with a non-null unrecorded_observation counts as open'. Then §7 gains a test that can fail: a fixture round of all-PASS rows where exactly one carries the field is not clean, and the same round with the field null is clean. Note also that a fixture proving the OLD behaviour must exist too -- rounds 10-13 as recorded are the fixture that must stay clean under today's rule.

finding: §5a rule (2) and §2 define the convergence population incompatibly, and neither section acknowledges the other. §2 states 'Both predicates are over non-PASS rows' and justifies that choice by a measurement I confirmed: across v0.35.0 and v0.36.0 every PASS row carries severity null (188/188, 195/195, ... 81/81; 0 rows anywhere omit the key). §5a then makes some PASS rows block. Such a row is non-blocking-by-construction under §2's predicate (its severity is null, which is not error, warning or info), so under audit_converge_on=blocking a PASS-with-observation is either always clean -- silently voiding rule (2) whenever the default is in force -- or always blocking, which is a fourth severity class the spec never introduces. Two engineers write opposite tests here, and one of them writes a test that passes while the mechanism it targets is inert.
suggestion: State the interaction in one sentence in §2 or §5a and test it both ways: whether a PASS row flagged under §5a blocks under `blocking`, under `all`, or both. If it should always block, say that it is exempt from the severity gate and give the reason; if it should carry a severity, say which values are legal on a PASS row and how that squares with the schema line 'severity: null for PASS'.

finding: §3's mechanism names a vocabulary the spec never binds to a stored field, and it contradicts the shipped predicate of the same name. What tp actually writes is `resolved: {status, evidence, resolved_at}` (internal/cli/audit_resolve.go:190-199) with status restricted to fixed|wontfix|duplicate (requireResolveStatus, :227-232). §3 says only 'a row carrying a wontfix or duplicate disposition', never naming `resolved.status`, so test 5 ('a row dispositioned wontfix') cannot be turned into an assertion without guessing the key. Worse, the shipped `rowDisposed` (internal/engine/unitkind.go:246-253) is deliberately status-blind -- '_, disposed := row["resolved"]' -- so it already treats a `fixed` row as disposed, which is exactly what §3 says must NOT happen for counting. §3 does not say whether rowDisposed changes, whether the resolve/audit-fix unit predicate keeps its current meaning, or how a row whose disposition status is unreadable is treated (dispositionStatusOf, :203-210, returns the string 'unknown' for that case).
suggestion: Pin the field path (`resolved.status`), the excluded value set ({wontfix, duplicate}), and the treatment of a `resolved` object with an absent, non-string or unknown status (the conservative reading -- not excluded -- matches the rest of tp's conventions and should be stated, not inferred). Say explicitly whether engine.rowDisposed keeps its status-blind meaning for units while convergence gets a status-aware one, and if so, name both predicates so a reader cannot confuse them.

finding: Tests 2, 3 and 5 all assert one surface and can pass while the counter the release's own §5 and §5b say the shipping rule reads stays broken. The same non-PASS predicate feeds two independent consumers: countAuditFindings (internal/cli/audit_record.go:248) produces the round's `findings`/`clean`, and auditRoundOpenByRole (internal/engine/rolestreaks.go:128-142) produces role_streaks[].open, which SpecCoverageCleanRounds reads to emit spec_coverage_clean_rounds. AuditRowIsPass's doc comment (internal/engine/auditrounds.go:43-46) states that the two 'must stay identical ... were the two to drift, the per-role open counts and the round's own stored findings would disagree about the same rows'. §3 changes only 'the round's finding count' and §2 speaks only of a round being clean. So an implementation that excludes a wontfix row from `findings` while role_streaks still counts it open passes test 5 exactly as written, and a round can report clean:true under `blocking` while spec_coverage_clean_rounds is 0 because spec-coverage's open count still includes three warnings -- which inverts §5's whole complaint instead of fixing it.
suggestion: Extend tests 2, 3 and 5 to assert the paired observable: for the same fixture round, `findings`/`clean` AND role_streaks[].open AND spec_coverage_clean_rounds must all agree about the same row. State in §2 and §3 whether the severity gate and the disposition exclusion apply to the per-role open counts too; if they deliberately do not, say so and amend AuditRowIsPass's doc comment, because it currently forbids that drift.

finding: No test asserts that every consumer of audit convergence reads audit_converge_on, which is the failure mode §5 is complaining about. Its twin has at least five consumers -- internal/cli/review_record.go:45, internal/cli/review_status.go:36, internal/cli/budget.go:18, engine.ReviewConverged (internal/engine/reviewclean.go:130-136) and the resume/run oracle -- and audit today routes through a different, severity-blind pair (engine.Converged / engine.ConsecutiveClean, internal/engine/reviewstate.go:429-511) whose doc comments say in as many words 'audit sequences keep using ConsecutiveClean' and 'audit convergence keeps using Converged'. Tests 1-3 as written are satisfied by wiring audit_converge_on into --record alone, leaving `--status --check`, `tp resume`'s oracle and `tp run`'s stop reasons blocking on advisory rows -- i.e. the release ships and the operator still cannot ship on --check.
suggestion: Add a test that sets audit_converge_on=blocking on a fixture whose only non-PASS rows are warning/info and asserts the SAME verdict from every surface: tp audit --record's payload, tp audit --status, tp audit --status --check's exit code, and tp resume's phase. List the consumers in §2 so decomposition produces one task per surface rather than one task for the predicate.

finding: Three of the seven substantive sections -- §5, §5a, §5b, roughly 100 of 288 lines -- have no entry in §7 and no entry in §6, so nothing says whether they ship in v0.37.0, and nothing could fail if they were dropped. §5 is the sharpest case: it states 'What this release must decide', then declines to decide ('The candidate shapes, neither chosen here'), and then states a test. But its two candidates are observationally different -- a `converge_roles` workflow field emits new config and changes what --check reads, whereas 'a --check that reports the shipping predicate itself with the all-roles count demoted to advisory' changes the payload shape and no config -- so two engineers implementing to §5 produce different JSON contracts and both satisfy the sentence. §5b likewise states a defect and 'the cheap answer' with no requirement, no test, and no non-goal.
suggestion: For each of §5, §5a, §5b, do one of two things and nothing else: choose the mechanism and add its numbered test to §7, or move it to §6 with the release that takes it named (§5b already points at spec/0.46.0.md §8 for provenance and could point there for delivery). If §5's choice is genuinely deferred, the honest form is a Non-Goal that says --check keeps its current all-roles meaning in v0.37.0, not a 'must decide' with no decision.

finding: The v0.36.0 row of §2.1's table is stale by six rounds, and the same spec contradicts it two sections later. The table says '7 and open'; spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/state.json records 13 audit rounds (audit-round-1..13.ndjson all present), and §5's own table cites rounds 10-13 while §2.0a cites 'rounds 12 and 13'. Re-derived under the stated predicate: r2 and r3 carry zero error rows, so 'converges at round 3' still holds; `all` is still 'not yet' (no round of the 13 is fully PASS). But the case AGAINST the default is understated -- r12 and r13 each carry 2 error rows, so `blocking` would have shipped over three separate error-bearing rounds (7, 12, 13), not one. This is the table the release's single contested decision rests on.
suggestion: Re-derive the row from state.json at spec time and write it as '13 and open', with the error-bearing rounds named (7, 12, 13). Better, bind the claim to an artifact rather than a number, as CLAUDE.md's own rule asks: state the one-line derivation (count rows with status != PASS and severity == error per audit-round-N.ndjson) beside the table so a later reader can re-run it instead of trusting a figure that goes stale between rounds of the very cycle that produced it.

finding: §4's mechanism and test 6 are unwritable as assertions on four counts. (1) 'resets consecutive_clean to zero' names a quantity that is not stored: engine.ConsecutiveClean (internal/engine/reviewstate.go:429-438) recomputes live from rounds[i].Clean on every call, so there is nothing to reset -- the implementable form is a stop condition in that walk, and the two differ observably on later rounds. (2) Test 6 says the reset is reported 'on the machine-readable surface' without naming a key; every other signal in this area is a named key (required_clean_rounds, role_streaks, spec_coverage_clean_rounds, divergence), so this one must be too. (3) It does not say which surfaces report it -- only the --record payload that observed the change, or --status thereafter. (4) The existing engine.Converged already ANDs !StateStale(rounds, currentHash) (reviewstate.go:509-511), so a spec-change guard is already in the audit path; §4 does not say whether it stays, and §1's 'audit has no equivalent' is loose about that.
suggestion: Re-state the mechanism as a walk rule ('the trailing clean-round walk stops at a round whose spec_hash differs from its successor's'), name the emitted key and its value (e.g. streak_reset: {reason: "spec-changed", at_round: N} or null) and say which commands emit it, and state explicitly that Converged's StateStale term is unchanged. Then test 6 becomes an equality assertion instead of a keyword search.

finding: §4's rule is pairwise ('a spec_hash different from the previous round's') and three edges it must decide are unstated, one of which is the loophole its own threat model describes. (a) Amend-then-revert: hash A -> B -> A. Under the pairwise rule the streak resets twice; under a 'count only rounds carrying the current spec_hash' rule the pre-change rounds resurrect and the streak survives. §1's stated threat is 'an agent can amend the spec to match code it just wrote and keep its clean-round streak', and revert-after-record is the cheapest way to do exactly that, so the two readings differ precisely where it matters. (b) The first recorded round has no predecessor -- reset or not. (c) §4 says the reset and spec/0.45.0.md's --reconcile 'compose' and that neither is a prerequisite, but not whether a reconciled move still resets; a reader can take 'reconcile explains the change' as 'reconcile excuses it'.
suggestion: State the rule over the whole recorded history rather than pairwise, add the first-round case in one clause, and add a §7 test for the A -> B -> A sequence with the expected streak value spelled out. On --reconcile, one sentence: a reconciled change resets the streak exactly as an unreconciled one does (the reconcile record is for the reader, not for the counter) -- or the opposite, if that is the intent, but it must be written.

finding: §5 pins its fixture on a status vocabulary the rest of the release does not use, so two engineers build different fixtures. The row vocabulary is PASS|PARTIAL|FAIL (audit_schema.go:20). §2, §3 and the whole counting mechanism are phrased on non-PASS; §5's test says 'another role has open non-FAIL rows'; and the CLAUDE.md rule §5 is reconciling with is phrased on a third quantity, 'no round has produced a FAIL'. A PARTIAL row is non-PASS and non-FAIL at once, so 'open non-FAIL rows' is satisfiable two ways and the exit-0 expectation differs between them. Worth recording that the fixture itself is producible -- v0.36.0 rounds 10-13 are literally it: spec-coverage open=0 for four consecutive rounds while maintainability-conventions carries 2/1/2/3 open rows, all PARTIAL or FAIL, and I reproduced §5's table exactly from those files -- so this is a wording defect, not a missing-fixture one.
suggestion: Rewrite §5's test on one vocabulary: 'the conformance role has zero non-PASS rows for required_clean_rounds consecutive rounds while another role has at least one non-PASS row'. Then say separately whether the shipping predicate's 'no FAIL' half is part of what --check would report, since that half is about status FAIL specifically and is the one place the two vocabularies genuinely both appear. Use spec/.tp-review/0.36.0 rounds 10-13 as the named fixture -- it is committed, it is the case the section argues from, and it costs nothing to construct.

finding: Test 4 pins two literal round numbers against mutable repository state and does not say how it reads it. spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/ is live loop state: recording a tenth audit round there, or editing any of the nine ndjson files, flips the expected values, and a snapshot-audit-round-10.md already exists in that directory from a round that was emitted but never recorded -- so a tenth entry is not hypothetical. Test 4 also must not invoke tp against the live spec: scripts/check-suite-state.sh wraps the suite in a before/after hash of spec/.tp-review/ precisely because a test that runs tp on a spec still sitting in the repository advances rounds it does not own (v0.36.0 §6.1 S1). §7 says the replay 'reads status and severity off recorded rows and needs no spec snapshot', which is the right property, but it stops short of saying the test is read-only and never calls tp against spec/0.35.0.md.
suggestion: Say in test 4 that the replay is a pure function over copies of the recorded rows -- read-only, no tp invocation against the live spec, or a relocatedSpec-style copy into t.TempDir() -- and derive the expected round numbers from a stated rule rather than pinning 3 and 9 as literals, so the test fails loudly with a wrong verdict rather than silently with a longer history. I verified the current numbers hold: for 0.35.0, rounds 2 and 3 carry zero error rows and rounds 8 and 9 are 200/200 PASS.

finding: §5b's 'cheap answer' silently reverses a shipped invariant that was chosen deliberately, and its observable is unpinned, so it cannot be tested either way. The proposal is that a round 'carry forward the roles it did not receive, marked as not-run rather than dropped, so a streak can neither advance nor vanish on their behalf'. The shipped rule is the opposite by design: ComputeAuditRoleStreaks documents 'A role with no rows in a round is not clean in it: the role was not measured, so cleanliness cannot be claimed for it, and the round therefore ends that role's streak instead of being skipped over ... the conservative direction -- they reset the signal toward keep auditing rather than toward you may ship' (internal/engine/rolestreaks.go:33-40). Carrying a streak across a round that did not measure the role means spec_coverage_clean_rounds can report 3 on the strength of a round that measured no conformance at all -- which is the ship rule reading a number nothing in that round supports. §5b does not name the tension, does not say what role_streaks emits for a not-run role (consecutive_clean carried forward? open null? a new field?), and uses 'should' rather than a requirement, so a decomposer cannot tell whether it ships.
suggestion: Decide between three observably different behaviours and write the one you mean plus its test: (a) keep today's reset and instead make the ABSENCE loud -- role_streaks carries an entry {role, status: "not-run"} for every role in the corpus that contributed no rows, and spec_coverage_clean_rounds stays null, which fixes 'the role is not reported as skipped or as stale' without touching any counter; (b) carry the streak forward and state explicitly that the conservative invariant is being traded away, with the reason; (c) refuse the narrow round at record time. (a) is the smallest and contradicts nothing. Whichever ships, pin the emitted JSON, because §5b's complaint is about what the payload says, not about arithmetic.

finding: Test 1 cannot be written deterministically: neither the precedence layers nor the exit code is pinned, and its twin has two different refusal paths with two different codes. 'Resolves through the documented precedence' does not say which layers apply -- review_converge_on has no CLI flag and no env var; it is settable at the task layer (internal/cli/set.go:45,371-376) and the project layer (internal/cli/set_project.go:64-69) only, so the generic CLI > env > task > project > built-in chain has two live layers here and three inapplicable ones. And 'an illegal literal is refused with the hint naming both legal values' collapses two shipped behaviours: tp set rejects a literal with ExitUsage/2 (set.go:374-376), while a CONSUMING command rejects an already-stored illegal value with ExitValidation/1 (review_record.go:45-49, review_status.go:36-40). Both are 'refused with the hint'; they are different tests.
suggestion: Split test 1 into three: (1) default resolves to blocking with no configuration; (2) tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=bogus and tp set --project ... exit 2 with the hint naming blocking and all; (3) a stored bogus value winning resolution makes each consuming audit command exit 1 with the same hint. Name the two layers that actually exist for this field in §2 rather than pointing at the five-layer chain.

finding: The one stated safety condition on the contested default has no mechanism in this release and is delegated to a spec that does not exist yet. §2.0a says a severity gate 'must not become a default stop at round 3 that ends rounds which would have changed their own method', cites v0.36.0 rounds 12 and 13 as the case (I confirmed: 2 error rows in each, on a cycle whose spec-coverage role had been clean since round 10), and then answers it by pointing at spec/0.49.0.md §1c. Per CLAUDE.md's own release plan 0.49.0 is last of thirteen and still pre-design. So the release ships a default whose stated precondition is owned by nothing, is in no §6 Non-Goal, and has no test. A 'must not' with no owner is the shape a later cycle re-derives from scratch.
suggestion: Either accept the risk in §6 explicitly ('this release ships blocking knowing it would have stopped v0.36.0's audit before rounds 12-13; the mitigation is spec/0.49.0.md §1c and is not part of v0.37.0'), or ship the cheap in-release mitigation and test it: when a round converges under blocking with non-blocking rows still open, --check and --record say so on the machine-readable surface (a nonblocking_open count and the roles carrying them), so the stop is visible rather than silent. The second is testable this cycle; the first at least stops the condition from reading as a requirement nobody implemented.

finding: Tests 7 and 8 are the two entries in §7 that cannot fail for the reason they are there. Test 8 ('a cycle whose spec never changes records an identical streak to today's') passes unchanged if §4 is never implemented at all, so it is only informative beside a test 6 that can fail -- and test 6 currently cannot, because no key is named (see the §4 row). Test 7 ('the reset does not delete or rewrite any recorded round') needs scoping: tp audit --record necessarily appends an entry to state.json and writes a new round file, so 'does not rewrite' has to mean the entries recorded BEFORE this invocation, compared field-by-field.
suggestion: Keep both, and make them falsifiable: test 8 as a differential -- the same fixture recorded twice, once with an unchanged spec and once with a changed one, asserting the streak differs between the two runs; test 7 as a byte comparison of the prior audit_rounds entries (round, file, findings, clean, spec_hash, roles_hash, recorded_at) before and after the reset-triggering record. On the recommendation the brief asks for: leave test 8 in -- it is the only clause defending against an over-eager reset -- but it earns its place only in the differential form.
